record.name: Assess models for genetic perturbation experiments
record.description: Which prediction methods and controls should I test before using expression predictions to plan genetic perturbation experiments?

attributes.question: Which prediction methods and controls should I test before using expression predictions to plan genetic perturbation experiments?
attributes.decision: Choose models and controls for a pilot in the intended cell system before using predictions to select follow-up experiments. The current evidence compares expression prediction; it does not establish experimental hit rates.
inputs: Single-cell expression measurements from perturbed and unperturbed cells, with perturbation and cell-type labels
A study design with multiple measured perturbations and cells per perturbation; combinations require combination examples during GEARS training
attributes.output: Predicted post-perturbation expression and changes relative to unperturbed controls, assessed against measured responses.
attributes.setting: Research method assessment anchored to the Norman2019 K562 cell-line comparison in GEARS Supplementary Table 6. Both endpoints below describe the same four evaluated configurations.
exclusions: Cross-cell-type transfer and bulk-sequencing prediction are outside the cited GEARS usage scope.
Training GEARS only on single-gene perturbations does not support reliable combination prediction.
Expression prediction scores do not establish causal mechanism, fitness effects or successful experimental prioritisation.
attributes.clinical_scope: Research use only. These expression endpoints do not establish diagnostic, treatment-selection or patient-response validity.
evidence_gaps: The exact Table 6 split manifest, scoring gene subset, scored counts and checkpoint revisions remain unextracted. Do not silently label the MSE endpoint as Top20.
The table does not identify its printed spread as SD, SE or a confidence interval; these scores do not establish a statistically supported winner.
Both endpoints and the repeated No Perturb row are overlapping evidence from one source comparison, not independent replications.
Performance in a new cell system and experimental hit rates need a separate prospective evaluation. Human scientific review remains outstanding.
30 September 2026 audit: A benchmark exists for expression responses, but prospective experiment-selection hit rates and transfer to a new cell system remain uncovered by this mapped comparison.
30 September 2026 audit: Table 6 scoring gene set, checkpoint revisions and exact split manifests remain unextracted; do not infer Top20 MSE or confidence intervals from the printed spreads.

Ahlmann-Eltze et al. 2025 (Nature Methods) prints no per-method value. Its per-model means for Fig. 1a, Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 2a and 8a are computed by Rewire from the authors' Source Data rows, not printed. Fig. 2c (bootstrapped ratios to the mean baseline, including the linear models with pretrained embeddings) is not extracted because its aggregation is ambiguous. The single-perturbation Source Data carry evidence concerns: the Fig. 2 legend counts are split 1 only and the Methods counts match no sheet.
Control-aware metrics (Systema, Nature Biotechnology 2025) are reported only in figures; no printed per-method values were found in this pass.

The one extracted multi-method comparison (Csendes et al. 2025) uses one GEARS perturbation-exclusive split per dataset with no spread; its authors, all employees of one company, built the baselines and re-ran the foundation models.

For Norman, Csendes et al. 2025 does not print how many training perturbations are combinations, so its combination results cannot be checked against the requirement for combination examples in GEARS training.
PerturBench combination-prediction results are in the store as task records and need a protocol before they can be judged for this use case.

record.name: Rank close analogues of a hit by binding affinity
record.description: Which method ranks a hit's close analogues by binding affinity accurately enough to choose what to make next, and at what compute cost against free energy calculation?

attributes.question: Which method ranks a hit's close analogues by binding affinity accurately enough to choose what to make next, and at what compute cost against free energy calculation?
intended_users: Medicinal chemists choosing which analogues of a confirmed hit to synthesise next
Computational chemists deciding whether to spend free energy calculation on a series
Project leads budgeting compute against synthesis in a lead-optimisation campaign
attributes.decision: Choose which analogues of a confirmed hit to make next, and choose the method and compute budget used to rank them.
inputs: A confirmed hit and a set of close analogues, with the series' chemical relationship stated
A protein structure or sequence for the target, and its relationship to any structure used in training
Measured affinities for part of the series, with the assay type and units recorded
An available compute budget and a synthesis budget
attributes.output: A ranking of the analogues by predicted binding affinity, with an error estimate against measured affinities on comparable series, the leakage control that estimate rests on, and the compute cost of producing it.
attributes.setting: Research-stage lead optimisation within one target's congeneric series. Ranking across unrelated targets, hit discovery from a large library and absolute affinity prediction are separate questions.
exclusions: No reviewed source in this batch publishes a per-series affinity-ranking value for any method: every extracted number is an average across series, so none of them says how well a given series would be ranked.
A correlation pooled or averaged over unrelated targets does not answer this question and flatters every method.
Accuracy on a benchmark series does not establish that a chosen analogue will be more potent, nor that it will be developable.
IC50, Ki and Kd are not interchangeable; sources that convert between them do so under a stated assumption that must be carried with the number.
Compute-cost comparisons are only meaningful against a measured alternative. The extracted tables print no measured cost for FEP+.
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Affinity ranking does not establish efficacy, safety or clinical suitability.
evidence_gaps: Automated source review only; independent human scientific review remains outstanding.

No reviewed source in the store publishes per-series affinity-ranking values for any machine-learning method. Every value recorded for a machine-learning method is a mean over series, so the question 'would this method have ranked my series correctly' cannot be answered from the store, only 'on average across these series'.

Per-series values are recoverable for the baselines but not for the machine-learning arms. The public_binding_free_energy_benchmark repository (MIT, releases v1.0 and v2.0) holds FEP+ per-edge results and the OpenFE per-transformation deposits on Zenodo cover the OpenFE arm; nothing was computed from either in this pass. The Boltz repository publishes no affinity predictions: at commit b1ebfc46ecf57f5414e0d1a6f9027bbb122c53bc its README and docs/evaluation.md still list the FEP+, CASP16 and MF-PCBA affinity predictions and the Boltz-2 evaluation scripts as 'coming soon'.
A comparison must not mix the two granularities: published per-series FEP+ values cannot be set beside Boltz-2's series averages in one comparison.

No fully independent evaluation of a machine-learning affinity predictor against free energy calculation on the same measured congeneric series was found. Both same-series comparisons that exist are reported by the developers of the machine-learning method, and both take their FEP+ arm from a benchmark whose protocol was tuned per system after seeing the error against experiment.

The peer-reviewed OpenFE industry benchmark (doi 10.1021/acs.jcim.6c00089) is behind an ACS paywall and was not retrieved, so the open-source free energy arm rests on a blog post the Boltz-2 supplement cites.
No measured compute cost for FEP+ exists in any extracted table; the only cost column prints '-' for FEP+ and ranges for OpenFE and ABFE.
No uncertainty is printed for any Boltz-2 supplement cell; the bootstrap error bars are figure-only.
The CASP16 assessors' per-group and per-target Kendall tau values are figure-only and were not extracted; the official per-target results file was not downloaded.

Neither the Merck FEP benchmark (Schindler et al. 2020) nor the Hahn et al. 2022 benchmark-construction paper nor the Wu et al. 2025 ABFE protocol paper was retrieved, so the series definitions behind the four-target subset are not established.

MM/GBSA and docking-score comparators on congeneric series were not searched for beyond the arms the Boltz-2 supplement chose for itself; recent affinity models other than Boltz-2, GAT and BACPI were not covered.
The overlap between the 876-complex OpenFE subset and the 87-compound four-target subset is not stated in any source, so the two comparisons cannot be treated as independent.

record.name: Use calibrated computational evidence for missense variants (PP3/BP4)
record.description: Which predictor and score thresholds give calibrated ACMG/AMP computational evidence (PP3/BP4) for a missense variant in a gene without a gene-specific calibration, and at what strength?

attributes.question: Which predictor and score thresholds give calibrated ACMG/AMP computational evidence (PP3/BP4) for a missense variant in a gene without a gene-specific calibration, and at what strength?
intended_users: Clinical scientists classifying germline variants under ACMG/AMP criteria
Variant curation expert panels deciding whether to adopt or replace genome-wide thresholds
attributes.decision: Choose one predictor in advance and the score thresholds at which it supplies PP3 or BP4 evidence at Supporting, Moderate or Strong strength, for a missense variant in a gene with no gene-specific calibration.
inputs: A germline missense variant on a stated transcript and genome build
The chosen predictor's precomputed score at a pinned version
Whether a gene- or region-specific specification exists that supersedes genome-wide thresholds
attributes.output: Calibrated score intervals for each evidence strength per predictor, the highest strength each reaches, the calibration data and its limits, and independent rankings of the same predictors. No variant classification.
attributes.setting: Germline missense variants assessed under ACMG/AMP criteria. The genome-wide calibrations use ClinVar pathogenic and benign missense variants rare in gnomAD, from genes with at least one pathogenic variant, with tools' training variants removed where available, and a prior probability of pathogenicity of 4.41% estimated from gnomAD.
exclusions: Genes with an expert-panel specification that sets its own thresholds (BRCA1/BRCA2 is a separate use case)
Splicing, in-frame indel, protein-truncating and non-coding variants
Combining several predictors, or counting PP3 together with overlapping evidence such as PM1 or allele frequency beyond the recommended caps
Somatic variant oncogenicity
Final variant classification or patient management
attributes.clinical_scope: Clinical research on the evidence strength of computational predictions. Calibrated thresholds hold on average across genes; they do not classify a variant and do not replace expert review.
evidence_gaps: The four tools that reach PP3_Strong in Pejaver et al. 2022 (BayesDel, MutPred2, REVEL, VEST4) each have a developer among that paper's authors; no independent recalibration of them is in the store.
The calibrations are genome-wide; Tejura et al. 2024 show that gene-level performance of REVEL and BayesDel often departs from them. No gene-level calibration is extracted.

Thirteen predictors have four-level intervals (Pejaver et al. 2022) and seven have points-scale intervals (Bergquist et al. 2025). Newer predictors ranked highly by Livesey and Marsh 2025 (for example popEVE, CPT-1) have no ClinGen calibration in the store.
Pejaver et al. 2022 Table S1 (point estimates and one-sided confidence bounds) was not retrieved.

A 2026 Genetics in Medicine calibration of machine-learning predictors (doi:10.1016/j.gim.2026.102606) is closed access and was not retrieved; the BayesQuantify (J Med Genet 2025) and P-KNN (bioRxiv 2025) joint calibrations were found but not extracted.
Evidence yield in real genomes (Stenton et al. 2024 Table 2) and reclassification impact (Dubé et al. 2026, Genet Med Open) were found but not extracted.
The Livesey and Marsh and ProteinGym rankings measure discrimination, not calibrated evidence strength; they help choose which predictors to calibrate, not which thresholds to apply.
Qualified human scientific review is outstanding; automated transcription does not establish replication.

record.name: Select a patient-RNA splicing-variant validation workflow
record.description: Which DNA/RNA evidence workflow identifies splice-altering variants for inherited-disorder follow-up when patient RNA and tissue-specific context are available?

attributes.question: Which DNA/RNA evidence workflow identifies splice-altering variants for inherited-disorder follow-up when patient RNA and tissue-specific context are available?
intended_users: Clinical researchers scoping the available diagnostic-genomics evidence
Computational researchers comparing exact evaluated configurations
attributes.decision: Inspect the FRASER known pathogenic-event recovery curve and the sequence-classification proxy evidence before selecting a workflow and designing patient-RNA follow-up for the intended cohort size.
inputs: Patient skin-fibroblast (or matched tissue) RNA-seq aligned reads
The number of samples available for a FRASER-style aberrant-splicing cohort
attributes.output: A sourced recovery curve (fraction of known pathogenic splicing events recovered as cohort size grows) and a separate sequence-classification proxy; no diagnostic-yield claim for unknown cases.
attributes.setting: FRASER, applied to a retrospective Kremer rare-mitochondrial-disorder skin-fibroblast RNA cohort (119 samples/105 individuals, 13 known pathogenic splicing events), recovers a mean 85% (11 of 13) of known events at a reduced 30-sample subsample. Separate, proxy sequence-classification results for DNA foundation models (Alavi et al. 2026: Evo 2 40B, Genos 10B and NTv3 650M classifying variants with established splicing defects against benign variants) are also linked, scoped as a different endpoint. Feng et al. 2025 Table 1 splice acceptor and donor classification is linked to 'Prioritise variants for splicing experiments', not here.
exclusions: Diagnostic yield in patients without a known pathogenic event (this is recovery of already-known events, not discovery)
Full-cohort outlier-gene workload counts (12/7/10 genes/sample), a different population from the 30-sample recovery evaluation and not ingested here
Blinded pathogenicity adjudication or VUS reclassification
attributes.clinical_scope: Clinical applicability is not established beyond known-event recovery. This does not demonstrate prospective diagnostic yield, blinded adjudication, or general tissue transfer.
evidence_gaps: No numeric confidence interval is reported for the 85% recovery figure in the inspected main text.
Subsampling repeat count and exact score-aggregation method are unextracted.

Feng et al. 2025 Table 1 splice-site classification is not linked to this use case: it measures AUC on benchmark splice-site sequences (DNABERT-2/NT datasets), not patient RNA, and is linked to 'Prioritise variants for splicing experiments'. The DNA foundation-model results linked here (Alavi et al. 2026: Evo 2 40B, Genos 10B and NTv3 650M) are threshold classifications of variants with established splicing defects, also proxies; none recovers events from patient RNA-seq.

AbSplice (Wagner et al. 2023, Nat Genet) reports its tissue-aware comparison with SpliceAI, MMSplice, SQUIRLS and CADD-Splice only in figures and prose in the copies screened, so no tissue-aware DNA predictor comparison is stored.
The FRASER 2.0 article (Scheller et al. 2023, AJHG) could not be retrieved as full text, and its comparison with FRASER, LeafCutterMD and SPOT on patient cohorts was not extracted.
No table comparing MMSplice, CADD-Splice or AbSplice against RNA-validated variants was found in this pass; Drost et al. cover SpliceAI, Pangolin, SPiP and SQUIRLS only.
Drost et al. variant-type strata (Data S1 Tables S5 and S6) are not extracted.
False positives are tabulated only as true-negative samples with any outlier (Silverstein et al. 2026, Table S9); outlier counts per sample remain figure-only.
Minigene or MFASS-style proxies beyond the existing MFASS mapping were not added in this pass.
MAJIQ-CLIN (Genet Med 2026) compares splicing outlier tools but could not be retrieved as full text.
Silverstein et al. 2026 expression-outlier true-negative counts conflict between Tables S7 and S9, so the OUTRIDER rows are not linked.
No machine-learning method has been compared with FRASER or OUTRIDER on the same patient RNA data in the linked evidence.

record.description: Which genetic perturbations should I test to produce a defined cellular response?

attributes.question: Which genetic perturbations should I test to produce a defined cellular response?
attributes.decision: Allocate a fixed experimental budget to perturbations most likely to produce the prespecified phenotype.
inputs: A defined cell system, starting state and target phenotype
Candidate genetic perturbations and a fixed testing budget
Measured perturbations and matched controls with guide, replicate and condition metadata
The intended transfer setting: unseen genes, combinations or a new cellular context
attributes.output: A ranked experimental shortlist with predicted phenotype effects, coverage and uncertainty about unmeasured conditions.
attributes.setting: Research selection for a defined genetic-perturbation screen. Chemical interventions and combinations need their own protocols. This question concerns phenotype hits rather than expression reconstruction alone.
exclusions: Transcriptome similarity alone does not establish successful experimental selection.
Generalisation to an unseen gene, combination and cell context must be evaluated separately.
Choosing experiments to maximise information gain is a separate decision.
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Predicted cellular responses do not establish patient response or treatment-selection validity.
evidence_gaps: 61 nominations / Results 57 selected targets / README 59 targets / 50 post-QC perturbations need reconciliation; no success fraction calculated.
Automated source review only; independent human scientific review remains outstanding.
Custom ranking AUC is not ROC AUC, prospective hit rate or efficacy.
No matched-budget conventional/random prospective comparison; no antitumor efficacy, rescue or selectivity result in this endpoint.
Original model implementations/checkpoints are not pinned in the intake; no uncertainty printed.
Preprint v1; original and reimplemented ranking scores kept separate. Screen2 ranking population is enriched by original nomination methods.

Matched random comparisons are retrospective only. AssayBench-Loop replays 20 screens with one random draw and prints no uncertainty; NAIAD's uniform arm still ranks pairs with the model, so the yield of testing randomly chosen pairs is not reported.
No prospective comparison of a model shortlist against random or conventional selection at the same budget.
The retrospective comparisons (AssayBench-Loop, NAIAD) were run by the developers of one of the compared methods; no independent replication.

Retrospective hits are each screen's own significance call. In AssayBench-Loop many recovered hits are common-essential genes, and the paper does not address whether the language models saw the test screens' publications in pre-training.
Combination evidence covers four two-gene viability screens only, gives the model every single-gene effect, and counts predicted as well as measured pairs as found.

attributes.question: Which methods recover causal variants and genes within a realistic laboratory review budget?
attributes.decision: Choose methods for prioritising variants in an initial exome or genome analysis, using phenotype, pedigree and molecular evidence to focus laboratory review.
inputs: Quality-controlled variant calls, genome build and calling coverage
Phenotype terms, pedigree, inheritance and available family sequencing
Dated population-frequency and gene–disease evidence
attributes.output: A ranked candidate list with supporting evidence, conflicts, filter reasons and unresolved findings for professional review.
attributes.setting: Initial ES/GS interpretation in a defined congenital-anomaly or developmental-disorder population. Singleton and family-based analysis require separate comparisons.
exclusions: Variant ranking alone does not establish pathogenicity or a patient diagnosis.
Balanced pathogenic/benign variant classification does not measure case-level diagnostic performance.
Reanalysis, cancer-risk estimation and treatment selection are separate questions.
attributes.clinical_scope: Clinical research on interpretation support. Confirmed diagnoses and downstream management outcomes require separate evaluation from candidate retrieval.
evidence_gaps: Known callable diagnosis recovery is available, but no controlled addition of a molecular-effect model at identical review effort was established.
Family, site and temporal independence, calling failures and unresolved outcomes need explicit prospective evaluation.
Talos/Exomiser comparison has source denominator discrepancies (194 body versus 190 extended figure); rank limits are not equal effort.
Qualified human scientific review remains outstanding; automated source transcription does not establish experimental replication.

No multi-tool comparison on 100kGP, UDN or CAGI cohorts with printed top-k values was found in this pass. The direct evidence comes from one laboratory group (Yuan et al. 2022 and 2024) on the DDD cohort and on its own in-house cohort.

Top-k recovery is measured only on solved cases with a single causal gene; no added source reports ranking on an unselected or unsolved cohort, so the recovery rates are likely higher than in routine use.
Candidates per case (review workload) is not reported by the added sources; only top-k recovery of a known causal gene.
Yuan et al. 2024 chose its Exomiser, PhenIX and AMELIE settings on the same cohorts it reports, and shows what separates Exomiser and PhenIX Protocols C and D only in a figure.

LLM evidence is limited to GPT-4 on synthetic candidate gene sets (Kafkas et al. 2025), and that study does not state which zero-shot prompt produced its table; no LLM was evaluated on real exome candidate lists.
Reese et al. 2026 (EJHG) compares seven LLMs with Exomiser on 5,213 phenopackets, but reports per-model values only in text and figures, and ranks diseases rather than genes or variants.

record.name: Select regulatory variants and genes for functional follow-up
record.description: Which variants, regulatory elements and genes should I perturb to explain a disease-associated locus?

attributes.question: Which variants, regulatory elements and genes should I perturb to explain a disease-associated locus?
attributes.decision: Choose allele edits, regulatory-element perturbations and gene readouts that can distinguish competing explanations for a locus.
inputs: Fine-mapped variants with genome build, ancestry and linkage-disequilibrium context
Candidate regulatory elements, genes and a relevant cell type
Sequence and available chromatin, expression or contact measurements
The feasible perturbation assay, readout and follow-up budget
attributes.output: A prioritised set of variant–element–gene hypotheses, with the experiments needed to test each link and effect direction where supported.
attributes.setting: Research follow-up of defined disease-associated loci in a specified cell system. Allele-effect prediction, element–gene linking and experimental shortlist selection are separate comparisons.
exclusions: Reporter activity does not by itself establish endogenous regulation.
Perturbing an entire regulatory element is different from editing one allele.
A regulatory link alone does not establish a gene’s causal role in disease.
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Molecular effects and regulatory links do not establish clinical variant classification or diagnostic validity.
evidence_gaps: Automated source review only; independent human scientific review remains outstanding.
No allele-specific endogenous-edit benchmark or equal-budget prospective shortlist benefit established.
Training/test independence unresolved: paper explicitly says benchmarking pipeline does not perform cross-validation.

No locus-to-gene comparison with printed per-method precision and recall was found. CALDERA (Schipper et al. 2026, PLoS Genet) prints only Brier scores for CALDERA, FLAMES, L2G and cS2G (Table 1); its AUPRC comparison is figure-only.

No benchmark of variant-effect predictors against endogenous allele edits (base, prime or saturation editing of noncoding sites) with printed per-method values was found; the linked variant comparisons use reporter assays.

The linked element-gene linking comparisons are by the developers of ENCODE-rE2G and ABC and their co-authors; the astrocyte CRISPRi benchmark (Green et al. 2026, Nat Neurosci), an independent test of ABC and ENCODE-rE2G, reports per-model values only in figures, prose and bootstrap source data.

No linked comparison scores long-context sequence models (Enformer, Borzoi) on reporter allelic effects with a documented input setup; Manzo et al. 2025 describe it two ways, so those rows are excluded.
Gschwind et al. Supplementary Tables 5 and 7 (eQTL and GWAS enrichment benchmarks) and the per-predictor K562 sheets of Table 3 are not extracted.
Manzo et al. causal-SNP top-k results within LD blocks are figure-only.

record.name: Prioritise variants for splicing experiments
record.description: Which evaluated configurations can inform selection of human SNVs for follow-up splicing experiments?

attributes.question: Which evaluated configurations can inform selection of human SNVs for follow-up splicing experiments?
intended_users: Experimental researchers selecting variants for functional follow-up
Clinical researchers investigating the limits of assay evidence
attributes.decision: Inspect the configurations evaluated against experimentally measured splicing of human SNVs (MFASS reporter assays, saturation minigene and genome-editing assays, and mini- or midigene tests), with their limitations, before selecting a method and designing validation in the intended experimental setting.
inputs: Human single nucleotide variants with alleles, genome assembly and gene/transcript context
The intended experimental endpoint and the number of variants that can be followed up
attributes.output: A sourced set of exact evaluated configurations and remaining validation needs; no patient-level variant classification or recommendation.
attributes.setting: Each linked comparison scores splice predictors against splicing measured in an experiment. MFASS measures exon recognition of human SNVs in an artificial minigene reporter; the matched study evaluates genomic-context SpliceAI and Pangolin configurations against this endpoint on a fixed held-out population. Saturation minigene assays and BRCA1 saturation genome editing measure every SNV in and around single exons, and mini- or midigene tests in HEK293T cells assess selected ABCA4 and MYBPC3 variants. Each source reports its own population, thresholds and metrics, and results are not pooled across sources.
exclusions: Indels and variant types outside the reviewed human SNV protocol
Patient-RNA effects, disease pathogenicity, diagnostic yield and treatment decisions
Pooling the matched annotation study with historical MFASS runs using other annotations or scoring populations
attributes.clinical_scope: Clinical applicability is not established. Reporter-assay ranking does not demonstrate patient-RNA performance, pathogenicity classification or clinical yield; validation in the intended population and workflow is still needed.
evidence_gaps: All four conditions scored 8,297 of 8,324 held-out variants. The same 27 exclusions comprise 23 hg19-to-hg38 assembly-orientation mismatches and four canonical-transcript-span exclusions; the latter are not established faulty variants. Missing predictions are not negative predictions.

No top-100 precision difference is established; Pangolin's masked top-100 result is sensitive to the registered tie order. Precision at 100 does not transfer automatically to another follow-up capacity or prevalence.
Individual-condition uncertainty intervals are not recorded. Paired-contrast intervals concern differences between conditions and must not be shown as each condition's uncertainty.
The study is exploratory: prior outcomes were inspected and nine contrast intervals are unadjusted. Matching annotation does not isolate model architecture.
Author confirmation of the assembly-orientation finding is not established. Human scientific review and independent replication remain outstanding.
These mappings do not change the MFASS task's discovered status. A source-reviewed applicability mapping is separate from reviewing the task record.
30 September 2026 audit: The four matched conditions exclude the same 27 of 8,324 held-out variants; missing scores are not negative predictions.

30 September 2026 audit: Historical v2 marginal scores have different scored subsets/annotations and require their own paired comparisons. Constant-prior top-100 counts reflect tied-score order. DNABERT2 is a pipeline rather than an exact configuration and remains outside the active mapping.

30 September 2026 audit: MFASS reporter exon inclusion does not validate patient RNA, diagnosis or prospective clinical follow-up. Human scientific review and external reproduction remain outstanding.

No linked source measures precision among the variants a tool would select for a new splicing experiment. The sources report sensitivity at a genome-wide background call rate (Smith and Kitzman 2023), classification at cutoffs tuned on the same data (Riepe et al. 2021), or ranking metrics on a whole assay cohort (Znabu et al. 2026).

Smith and Kitzman 2023 report sensitivity at transcriptome-normalised thresholds; precision and prAUC per tool and dataset are figure-only (Figure 3), and the 5% and 20% call-rate sheets and the sensitivity-AUC sheet of Table S2 are not extracted.
Riepe et al. 2021 Tables 3 to 5 do not state the cutoff applied; Table 2 cutoffs were optimised on the same data sets, so values may be optimistic.
Znabu et al. 2026 is a preprint scoring the whole labelled MFASS cohort; it is not comparable with the matched-annotation or v2 held-out MFASS protocols.
CAGI5 Vex-seq and MaPSy assessments (Mount et al. 2019) print per-submission values for challenge entries, most of which are not released tools; not extracted.
No independent printed comparison on Vex-seq or MaPSy for current tools (SpliceAI, Pangolin, SpliceTransformer) was found.
OpenSplice (bioRxiv 2026.05.22.727141) and SeqSplice BRCA1/BRCA2 (Genome Res 2025) are leads not screened for per-tool tables.

record.name: Choose structural hypotheses to guide experiments
record.description: Which predicted interfaces or structures are reliable enough to guide my next experiment?

attributes.question: Which predicted interfaces or structures are reliable enough to guide my next experiment?
intended_users: Researchers selecting interface mutations or protein constructs
attributes.decision: Choose structural hypotheses and associated mutations or constructs for experimental testing.
inputs: Protein sequences, partner identities and the intended assembly
Available experimental structures or templates with release dates
A defined experimental choice and testing budget
Relevant biochemical conditions and alternative conformations
attributes.output: Structural hypotheses with confidence and coverage estimates, linked to proposed mutations or constructs and tests of their reliability.
attributes.setting: Research planning within a bounded class of protein complexes. Monomers, antibody complexes and ligand complexes require separate comparison protocols.
exclusions: Structural accuracy alone does not establish that a proposed experiment will succeed.
High confidence does not prove interaction existence, affinity or function.
Results from one complex class do not establish performance in another.

Confidence scores do not separate real from non-cognate pairings: on nanobody-antigen complexes the best average precision was 0.187 against a 0.011 baseline, so a confident model is not evidence that the interaction exists.
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Structural hypotheses do not establish therapeutic efficacy or clinical suitability.
evidence_gaps: Automated source review only; independent human scientific review remains outstanding.
No intervals in Table 3; no prospective experimental utility or matched conventional mutation/construct baseline.

Scored target populations differ; Table 1 assessable counts are retained as coverage context, not verified metric denominators. Some Table 3 rates do not reconcile with integer counts after rounding. No complete-cohort estimate is inferred.

ClusPro uses component 3D structures and BM5 targets, so scores cannot be directly compared with FoldBench; BM4 parameter benchmarking limits holdout independence. Exact ClusPro revision and input hashes remain unextracted.

ClusPro Total/easy/top10 source prints 87 although subtotals and 51.68% imply 77; literal 87 is retained as needs_review outside use-case mappings. Antibody and aggregate classes are not mapped to this issue.
Confidence selection is tested only for AlphaFold3 on antibody-antigen complexes (Fromm et al. 2026); no equivalent table was found for Boltz, Chai-1, protein-protein or protein-ligand complexes.
The nanobody evidence is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, pools systems inside and outside each tool's training data, and defines its negatives as untested shuffled pairings.
No linked comparison reports uncertainty intervals for per-tool values.
No linked comparison connects a predicted structure or confidence score to the outcome of an experiment.
No machine-learning method has been compared with ClusPro docking on the same protein-protein data in the linked evidence.

record.name: Select therapeutic targets for validation
record.description: Which targets should I test to change a defined disease-relevant phenotype?

attributes.question: Which targets should I test to change a defined disease-relevant phenotype?
attributes.decision: Select targets and modulation directions for a validation batch, with clear tests of the proposed disease mechanism.
inputs: A defined disease, biological context and experimental phenotype
A candidate gene set and feasible ways to inhibit or activate each target
Dated genetic, expression and functional evidence, including conflicting findings
A validation budget and relevant normal-cell or selectivity controls
attributes.output: A shortlist of target–disease–intervention hypotheses with supporting evidence, uncertainties and proposed validation experiments.
attributes.setting: Research planning for one disease and a prespecified experimental system. The intended comparison tests whether rankings improve the yield of useful target effects.
exclusions: Untested targets cannot be treated as negative examples.
Cellular dependency, target tractability and a therapeutic window require different evidence.
A target association does not establish that modulating it will benefit patients.
Recovering a published screen's own hits is not evidence that a nominated target is worth pursuing.
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Target prioritisation does not establish treatment benefit or support patient-specific treatment decisions.
evidence_gaps: 61 nominations / Results 57 selected targets / README 59 targets / 50 post-QC perturbations need reconciliation; no success fraction calculated.
Automated source review only; independent human scientific review remains outstanding.
Custom ranking AUC is not ROC AUC, prospective hit rate or efficacy.
No matched-budget conventional/random prospective comparison; no antitumor efficacy, rescue or selectivity result in this endpoint.
Original model implementations/checkpoints are not pinned in the intake; no uncertainty printed.
Preprint v1; original and reimplemented ranking scores kept separate. Screen2 ranking population is enriched by original nomination methods.

The multi-method comparisons added on 2026-10-09 are retrospective replays of published screens, not prospective validation batches: a method selects genes and the screen's existing measurement is looked up.

An independent replication reports that the agent compared in Roohani et al. 2025 performs about the same when its experimental feedback is replaced by randomly permuted outcomes (at least as high on three of five screens with each of three backbones), so its margin over the baselines should not be read as learning from each round's results.
No benchmark found scores target nominations against a therapeutic window, selectivity, dependency or tractability, and none establishes patient benefit.

AssayBench reports lower scores for most systems on screens published after the models' training cutoff, which its authors read as partly prior exposure to the literature; that cohort has 19 screens, and two systems score higher on it.
